name: Chin tucks

card.summary: A neck-retraction movement used for posture and deep neck flexor work; most published research concerns swallowing therapy, not jawline appearance.
card.aka: Neck retraction, McKenzie chin tuck, chin retraction
card.note: Research on chin tucks is mainly from swallowing studies; some forum users warn about prolonged holds.

quick.overview:
A chin tuck is a movement in which the head is drawn straight back so the chin moves toward the neck without tilting the head down. It is used in posture routines and aimed at the deep neck flexor muscles, and it is often paired in forums with rows and face pulls for forward head posture.
Published studies of chin tucks are mostly in swallowing (dysphagia) research, where the posture is used as a compensatory maneuver. Studies of its effect on facial appearance were not found.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say the movement strengthens the deep neck flexors and counteracts a head carried forward of the shoulders, which they link to a more defined jaw-neck profile. Swallowing studies show that the chin-tuck posture changes pharyngeal dimensions and pressure events.
quick.risks: No serious harms are documented. One looksmax.org thread author claims that holding a chin tuck for long periods could strain the cervical spine, a claim that other users in the thread called fear mongering; no study cited here tests it.

lead: A chin tuck is a movement in which the head is drawn straight back over the neck so that the chin moves in toward the throat while the gaze stays level. In appearance culture it is used to bring a forward-carried head back into line with the shoulders, which people say gives the jaw and the line from chin to neck a cleaner, more defined profile in photos and in person. It is usually done as a daily set of repetitions or holds, often against a wall, with a towel or band for resistance, and is frequently paired with neck curls, rows and face pulls [1][14][15][16].

In the clinical literature the term most often refers to a swallowing posture used with people who have dysphagia, and it has been studied with videofluoroscopy and manometry [1][2][3][4]. A resisted version, chin tuck against resistance (CTAR), was proposed in 2014 as a way to raise suprahyoid muscle activity [5]. Physical-therapy studies also use neck retraction, the same basic motion, as a posture and neck-pain exercise and as an endurance test for the neck flexors [17][18].

On looksmax.org the movement is discussed in connection with forward head posture, the hyoid area, a tighter submental profile and even voice resonance. Users post before-and-after photos, ask whether it is a 'cope' or 'real', and debate whether prolonged holds are safe [7][14][15][16]. Published studies have examined swallowing mechanics, neck-flexor endurance and neck-pain rehabilitation; none located has measured facial or jaw appearance as an outcome.

chain: Retract the head over the neck and strengthen the muscles at the front of the neck
Head sits less far forward of the shoulders
Claimed result: a cleaner chin-to-neck line and a more defined jaw in profile
angle.text: People use chin tucks, often with neck curls and rows, to correct a head that sits forward of the body, on the reasoning that a retracted head shows the jaw and neck line better from the side and in photos. The movement itself is well described in physical-therapy and swallowing research; the appearance payoff is what practitioners report from their own photos and experience [2][15].

paras: The movement involves retracting the head horizontally while keeping the gaze level, rather than nodding the head downward. The deep neck flexors, including the longus colli, lie in front of the cervical spine and flex the neck and head; Wikipedia notes their position also gives them a role in neck posture [21]. The movement is commonly done lying down, seated or standing against a wall, and progressed with light resistance from a towel, band or ball.

A looksmax.org user attributes a version called the McKenzie chin tuck to the orthotropics advocate Mike Mew and says it rotates the head into flexion [7]. The name McKenzie also appears outside looksmaxxing: a poster on T Nation asked a training-log author whether he had tried the 'McKenzie neck stuff' such as chin tucks and neck extensions for a neck complaint [25]. Strength athletes log banded chin tucks among rehab items alongside tendon and shoulder work [26].

Forward head posture is described by Wikipedia as a head position in which the ear sits ahead of a vertical line through the shoulder, tied to prolonged hunching over laptops and phones and to certain occupations. Its list of proposed remedies includes strengthening the deep neck flexors, mid and lower back and scapular retractors, stretching the muscles that pull the head forward, and ergonomic changes, with several statements flagged on the page as needing confirmation [6].

Appearance communities connect this to the face. A head carried forward can make the chin and neck appear to merge in profile; Wikipedia's article on double chin separately describes causes as excess neck fat or a bony deficiency in which the jaws do not project far enough, with treatments such as hyoid lift, genioplasty and orthognathic surgery [23]. Practitioners who do chin tucks say that bringing the head back is a free first step that changes how the jaw reads before any such procedure is considered.

The hyoid bone, which many forum users mention, is a horseshoe-shaped bone between the chin and thyroid cartilage anchored only by muscles and ligaments, with tongue, floor-of-mouth and throat muscles attached to it [20]. One looksmax.org poster who asked whether chin tucks and neck curls were 'cope or real' was told by replies that they were the best exercises for improving the hyoid area, and another said the aim was to 'raise hyoid' [14]. No published study located measures hyoid position change from these exercises.

Threads on looksmax.org ask whether chin tucks and neck curls help, how to perform them efficiently, whether they widen the jaw, and whether neck pain during the exercise is normal [14][27][28]. Posters describe daily routines of several sets, sometimes weighted with towels, and report improved posture over weeks [15].

One poster shared before-and-after photos and said that, at the same weight and facial fat, the difference after adding weight to chin tucks was clear; replies agreed that the exercise raises the hyoid [15]. Another poster reported that holding a chin tuck made the voice sound deeper and more resonant, and said a voice therapist had taught a related position for a pitch condition; the thread's replies included a mix of agreement and insults [16].

The practice sits next to mewing and other jaw-and-posture routines. Wikipedia describes mewing as oral posture training developed by orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike, spread widely on social media from about 2019 and associated with looksmaxxing subcultures, and notes that the American Association of Orthodontists states there is no evidence it improves the jaw [24]. Chin tucks are a separate, neck-focused movement, though they are often discussed in the same posture-and-jaw circles.

Most studies examine chin tuck as a swallowing posture. A manometry study of seven subjects compared neutral, head-turn and chin-tuck conditions for pharyngeal pressure events [1]. Videomanometry studies tested supraglottic swallow, effortful swallow and chin tuck in eight healthy volunteers and in eight patients with pharyngeal dysfunction [2][3]. A 2002 report from the same line of work examined hypopharyngeal intrabolus pressure [8]. A radiographic study of 30 subjects measured pharyngeal dimensions in neutral and chin-tucked positions [9], and a clinical and electrophysiologic study examined how head and neck positions affect oropharyngeal swallowing [10].

The resisted variant, CTAR, was described in a 2014 paper as a Shaker-type exercise designed to raise suprahyoid muscle activity [5]. Reviews of dysphagia management after stroke and swallowing rehabilitation after oropharyngeal cancer surgery mention chin-tuck-based approaches in rehabilitation contexts [11][12]. Wikipedia's dysphagia article groups postural techniques with compensatory procedures and lists resistance exercises and swallowing maneuvers among therapeutic ones [22].

Neck retraction, the same motion, appears in posture and neck-pain research. A 2005 repeated-measures study of 41 people with and without neck pain used an isometric neck-retraction test of neck-flexor endurance; mean endurance was about 39 seconds in the group without neck pain and about 24 seconds in the group with neck pain, and reliability was good to moderate [17]. A 2025 randomized trial in patients with mechanical neck pain gave all participants an 8-week neck-retraction exercise programme and found that adding cervical manipulation produced larger early changes in pain scores and range of motion [18]. A small 2021 experimental study of 14 young women with kyphotic posture compared two exercise sets, both containing cervical retraction, over four weeks [19]. These studies concern pain, endurance and spinal alignment, not facial or jaw appearance.

Chin tucks are described in the studies above as an ordinary rehabilitation movement and no serious harms are documented. A looksmax.org poster argues that the version promoted online can hyperflex the neck and, if held for long periods, strain discs, the spinal cord and occipital muscles; replies call this fear mongering and say chin tucks paired with face pulls strengthen the occipital region [7]. No study located has examined sustained chin-tuck holds. Another thread asks whether neck discomfort during the exercise is normal [27]. People with neck injuries or swallowing problems are generally managed by clinicians.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the chin tuck appears in threads asking whether it is 'cope or real', about hyoid position, jaw width, voice and neck safety [7][14][15][16].

claims.claim: Chin tucks improve head posture by stretching and strengthening the neck.
claims.believers: A forum reply says the movement stretches the neck and leads to better head posture, and a poster reports posture improving day by day with weighted tucks [13][15].
claims.experts: Neck retraction is used in physical-therapy studies of neck pain and alignment [17][18][19]; no study located tests facial appearance outcomes.

claims.claim: Chin tucks and neck curls raise the hyoid bone and improve the jaw-neck area.
claims.believers: Replies in looksmax.org threads say the exercises are the best ones for the hyoid area and that they 'raise hyoid' [14][15].
claims.experts: The hyoid is held by muscles and ligaments rather than joined to other bones [20]; no published study located measures hyoid position after chin-tuck training.

claims.claim: Chin tucks make the voice deeper.
claims.believers: A poster says holding a chin tuck made the voice more resonant, and describes a voice-therapy position related to it [16].
claims.experts: No published study located tests chin tucks for voice pitch or resonance.

claims.claim: Chin tucks or neck curls widen the jaw.
claims.believers: Forum users ask whether the exercises help the jaw get wider [28].
claims.experts: No published study located links chin tucks to jaw structure; swallowing studies examine pharyngeal pressure and dimensions [1][9].

claims.claim: Prolonged chin-tuck holds can damage the neck.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says the movement as promoted can cause hyperflexion and, if held for long, harm discs, spinal cord and occipital muscles; replies call this fear mongering [7].
claims.experts: No study located has examined harms from sustained chin tucks; trials use neck retraction as a supervised exercise [18].

claims.claim: Before-and-after photos show chin tucks changing the face.
claims.believers: A poster shares photos at equal weight and facial fat and says the difference is clear after adding weight to the exercise [15].
claims.experts: Photos vary with angle, lighting and head position; no controlled study of facial appearance after chin-tuck training has been published.
